title: tabagent: the TabAgent Python package
description:
The code of the paper TabAgent: Distilling LLM Agent Components into Cheap Classifiers (arXiv:2602.16429): the tabagent Python package, with TabSchema, TabSynth and TabHead, onboarding from agent logs, scikit-learn estimators, an HTTP decision service, and the commands that recompute the paper's public results. If you use it, please cite the paper.

Agentic systems chain LLM calls to make closed-set decisions: choosing from a fixed candidate set, as in skill selection, tool shortlisting, application selection, and routing. These repeated frontier-model calls dominate per-task latency and cost. We show such decisions need not be made by a language model at all: a compact discriminative head, trained on the agent's own successful execution traces, can replace the generative one while leaving the surrounding agent intact. TabAgent has three parts. (i) TabSchema extracts schema, state, and dependency features from trajectories. (ii) TabSynth adds schema-aligned synthetic rows where trajectory coverage is thin. (iii) TabHead, a cheap tabular classifier, scores candidates in a single pass. Changing only the label space, we test TabAgent as a drop-in replacement for the frontier-LLM heads (e.g., GPT-5.4) across three decision families and seven agent benchmarks. On tool shortlisting it recovers essentially all of the tools the GPT-5.4 shortlister used on its successful runs (Recall@9), at 99.96% lower latency and 99.9996% lower cost per call (~10^3x and ~10^5x). It also ranks first on the classification decisions and is on par with a strong fixed default on the harder routing and gating decisions at far lower latency and cost, where a costly generative router does worse. Across these tasks, the gains come from the representation, not the model: a discriminative head over raw text or embeddings alone collapses, and trace-derived features make it accurate.
